### Problem: Kth Largest Element in an Array {#sec-salgo-p3-a}

::: {.p-statement}

Given an integer array `nums` and an integer $k$ ($1 \le k \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^4 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 10^4$), return the $k$-th largest element **in the sorted order** (not the $k$-th distinct). LeetCode's follow-up dares you: *can you solve it without sorting?*

Source: [LC 215 · Kth Largest Element in an Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-largest-element-in-an-array/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example — `nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2`. Output `5` (sorted down: 6, **5**, 4, 3, 2, 1).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
You only asked for **one** rank. Sorting is a promise to place *every* element correctly — a promise you never cash. Quickselect makes only the promise you need: partition around a pivot, discover the pivot's final rank, and recurse into the single side that contains the target. Each partition throws away a whole side forever, so the expected work is $n + n/2 + n/4 + \dots = O(n)$.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Sort and index.** Sort descending and read position $k-1$. $O(n \log n)$, trivially correct — the oracle and the honest shipping choice.
2. **Quickselect.** Pick a pivot, three-way partition into `< pivot | == pivot | > pivot`, then recurse only into the block that holds index $n-k$ (the $k$-th largest from the left is the $(n-k)$-th smallest). Randomising the pivot keeps the $O(n)$ expectation away from the $O(n^2)$ sorted-input trap.

**Invariant.** After a partition the pivot occupies its final sorted position, so if that position is the target the answer is the pivot; otherwise the target lies wholly in the smaller or the larger block and the other can be discarded.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Sort and index

::: {.form-next}
Sort descending, return `nums[k-1]`. $O(n \log n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra in place. It is the baseline that any "without sorting" claim must beat.

**Worked example.** $[3,2,1,5,6,4], k=2$: sorted down $[6,5,4,3,2,1]$ → index 1 = $5$.
:::


::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def kl215_sort(nums, k):
    return sorted(nums, reverse=True)[k - 1]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// sort descending, read index k-1; O(n log n)
int kl215Sort(vector<int> nums, int k) {
    sort(nums.begin(), nums.end(), greater<int>());
    return nums[k - 1];
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** One sort, one index. The point of writing it is to have something the $O(n)$ form must agree with on every random input — the stress test below is exactly `kl215_qs(a, k) == kl215_sort(a, k)`.

#### Quickselect

::: {.form-next}
The $k$-th largest is the value that would sit at index $n-k$ if the array were sorted ascending. Quickselect finds it without sorting the rest: partition around a pivot, learn the pivot's home index, and recurse only into the side containing $n-k$. A three-way split (`< == >`) also absorbs duplicate-heavy inputs that would otherwise stall a two-way partition. Expected $O(n)$, worst $O(n^2)$ only for consistently unlucky pivots.

**Worked example.** $[3,2,1,5,6,4], k=2$: target index $n-k=4$. Pivot $4$ partitions to $[3,2,1]\mid4\mid[5,6]$; index 4 lives in the greater block $[5,6]$, whose local target is its smaller element $5$.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("kth", "qs")
    assert str(final) == "5"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-salgo-215-qs
def kl215_qs(nums, k):
    a = list(nums)
    target = len(a) - k                     # k-th largest == target-th smallest

    def select(lo, hi):
        p = a[random.randint(lo, hi)]        # random pivot -> expected O(n)
        lt, i, gt = lo, lo, hi               # in-place 3-way (Dutch) partition
        while i <= gt:
            if a[i] < p: a[lt], a[i] = a[i], a[lt]; lt += 1; i += 1
            elif a[i] > p: a[i], a[gt] = a[gt], a[i]; gt -= 1
            else: i += 1
        if target < lt:                      # answer is in the < p band
            return select(lo, lt - 1)
        if target > gt:                       # answer is in the > p band
            return select(gt + 1, hi)
        return p                              # target lands inside the == p band

    return select(0, len(a) - 1)

for _ in range(200):
    arr = [random.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 40))]
    kk = random.randint(1, len(arr))
    assert kl215_qs(arr, kk) == kl215_sort(arr, kk)
assert kl215_qs([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2) == 5
assert kl215_qs([3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], 4) == 4
print("kl215_qs OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// quickselect with in-place 3-way (Dutch) partition, expected O(n)
int kl215Select(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi, int target) {
    int pivot = a[lo + rand() % (hi - lo + 1)];   // random pivot index
    int lt = lo, i = lo, gt = hi;   // a[lo..lt-1] < p, a[lt..i-1] == p, a[i..gt] unseen, a[gt+1..hi] > p
    while (i <= gt) {
        if (a[i] < pivot)      swap(a[lt++], a[i++]);
        else if (a[i] > pivot) swap(a[i], a[gt--]);
        else                   ++i;
    }
    if (target < lt) return kl215Select(a, lo, lt - 1, target);
    if (target > gt) return kl215Select(a, gt + 1, hi, target);
    return pivot;                                  // target lands inside the ==pivot band
}
int findKthLargest(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    return kl215Select(nums, 0, n - 1, n - k);     // k-th largest = (n-k)-th smallest, 0-based
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The three buckets turn the array into `< pivot`, `== pivot`, `> pivot`; the running left-length tells you which band hides index `target`, and you recurse into just that band — the other two are never touched again. The `== pivot` band is why a three-way split is used: with many duplicates a two-way partition would keep re-choosing the same value and degrade to $O(n^2)$. Randomising the pivot is what makes the sorted-input and all-equal inputs safe.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Sort and index** is $O(n \log n)$ time; `sorted` makes an $O(n)$ copy, `std::sort` works in place with $O(\log n)$ stack. **Quickselect** is expected $O(n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra in place — each round discards a side, so the sizes form a geometric series. A min-heap holding the $k$ largest values is the third option: $O(n \log k)$, which wins when $k \ll n$ and is the right shape for the streaming sibling @sec-salgo-p4-b.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $k = 1$ (largest) and $k = n$ (smallest) are just the two extreme ranks; quickselect handles both.
- All equal → the three-way band swallows everything and returns the pivot at once.
- Without the random pivot, an adversarial sorted array makes the naive last-element pivot $O(n^2)$.
:::
